title: The White Lotus Does Not Whisper
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 23 of 40
content:
The White Lotus members arrived before the tea had finished steeping.

Not late. Not early. Exactly when Iroh had said they would, which should have been my first warning that this wasn't a social visit.

A woman in a travel-stained green coat set a game tile on the back-room table. Two men followed her. One of them looked toward me, then toward Iroh, as if I were a chair someone had forgotten to move.

"I can wait upstairs," I said.

"Do you want to?" Iroh asked.

"No. But I would like to know whether this is a conversation I'm allowed to hear."

The woman stopped unfastening her satchel. "That is a fair question."

Iroh put a fresh cup down for me. "Jasper is my guest, not my subordinate. You may ask for a private meeting. Please do not decide that the request has already been granted."

One of the men gave him a look full of old battles. "You still make everything difficult."

"Only the easy things."

The woman introduced herself as Scholar Ren. She had brought a list of travelers who needed discreet escort through Ba Sing Se, and a second list of supplies the White Lotus could not obtain without drawing the wrong attention. She did not offer me either list. I appreciated the distinction more than I expected.

"Then what can I do?" I asked.

"Nothing, if you don't wish to," Ren said. "We came to ask the general for help."

"I sell tea," Iroh said mildly.

"You also know which warehouses change their locks without announcing it."

His smile faded. For a moment I saw the man who had once commanded an army and later made a deliberate choice not to be that man again. Ren's hand remained on the satchel. Nobody reached for a weapon. The danger was in what the names on those papers could cost someone.

I carried the kettle to the stove. Mina had left the day's stock sheet under a paperweight. Three jars of jasmine, one open tin of roasted barley, two cracked cups marked for repair. The shop could not vanish into intrigue every time an old friend needed Iroh.

"Mina is covering the morning rush alone," I said. "If you need this room until noon, I can help her. If you need it until evening, we have a staffing problem."

Ren blinked. "We can return after closing."

Iroh looked at me, and his expression softened in a way I wasn't sure the visitors noticed.

"She doesn't get paid to be part of this," I added.

"I beg your pardon?" Ren said.

"Mina. Her time isn't free because the cause is important."

After a long pause, Ren closed the satchel. "After closing, then. And we'll pay for the tea."

"Extraordinary progress," Iroh said. "Perhaps next you will ask whether I am available."

I stayed in the shop while they arranged a later hour. Across the counter, a little boy was trying to trade three shiny buttons for a bun. Mina counted out the price and gave him a smaller roll he could actually afford, refusing Iroh's attempt to make the bakery budget disappear through generosity.

"You don't have to be kind with other people's stock," she told him.

"An excellent rule," I said.

"Then you should explain it to your boyfriend."

I nearly dropped the tray. Iroh laughed so hard he had to sit down.

Later, when the doors were shut and the final customer had gone, Ren came back alone. This time she asked whether I wanted to leave before she unfolded the map. I said yes to the identities, no to being excluded from every discussion about how the shop would be affected.

Iroh held out a chair.

"Does that mean you're joining the White Lotus?" Ren asked.

"No," I said. "It means I know where the spare lamp oil is, and I'm allowed to have an opinion about locking a public shop at the wrong hour."

The map showed a supply route. I helped calculate how much tea could be moved without leaving Mina short for the following week. Nothing about it made me an operative. There were portions of the plan I was not shown. I didn't insist. A boundary could be an act of care when it belonged to the people it protected.

After Ren left, Iroh turned the White Lotus tile over in his fingers.

"I feared you would think I was keeping a second life from you," he said.

"You are keeping parts of a life private. That's different from making promises you can't keep."

He watched me carefully.

"I've told you I'm ethically non-monogamous," I continued. "I prefer polyamory. I don't expect every person I care for to hand over their letters or their whole history. I do expect them to tell me when something changes our plans, our safety, or the promises we've made."

"You ask for honesty without ownership."

"I'm trying. I'm not always graceful at it."

"Neither am I."

I laughed. "That might be the first unwise thing you've said all day."

"Give me time."

He reached across the table, palm up. I laid my hand in his. For a little while he wasn't a general, a symbol, or the keeper of anybody's secret. He was tired, and a bit ridiculous, and warm beside me.

"Would you like to stay after the lamps are out?" he asked.

"Yes. But first, did you actually pay Mina for the extra hour?"

He closed his eyes. "I have been defeated by the greatest strategist in Ba Sing Se."

I kissed him gently, then took the account book off the shelf. We fixed the wages before going upstairs. The curtain fell across the back room, and the rest of the night belonged to us.
